Bitcoin is pumping, but US spot demand still isn’t confirming the move.

The Coinbase Premium is back below 0, meaning BTC trades slightly cheaper on Coinbase than on Binance.

That doesn’t guarantee a retrace, but without stronger spot buying, the rally could be easier for perp traders to fade.

IMO, 3 things need to happen:

1. The Coinbase Premium needs to reclaim zero.
2. It needs to remain positive, not just briefly cross above it.
3. Ideally, it should rise alongside BTC, showing that Coinbase buyers are supporting the move.

The rally can continue without this, but a sustained positive premium would make it much more convincing.

For now, I’m watching to see whether US spot demand catches up with the price.

I had my agents crank on this question for over a week. Together we investigated the 25 largest operating US AI campuses (according to Epoch), looking at satellite imagery, equipment, nearby homes, and noise complaints.

thread_tweets.text:
My approach was to evaluate each data center with satellite imagery, look at filings and identify the loudest equipment (typically cooling towers or gas turbines), find the nearest cluster of 5+ homes, and measure that distance. 

From those distances and assumptions about the equipment and the terrain, I was able to derive a modeled noise estimate in dBA. I compared this against a history of verified complaints for each data center.

thread_tweets.text:
The main thing that shocked me was how close some of these absolutely enormous facilities are to neighborhoods.

11 of the 25 are less than 500 meters from a residential cluster. The closest is about 90 meters.

Contrary to what I thought, these are not all remote campuses in the middle of nowhere. Some are practically in people’s backyards.

thread_tweets.text:
Proximity isn’t destiny.

For 17 of the 25, I found no credible current operating noise complaint. 

Four had limited allegations or substantially remediated issues. Four had more substantial documented concerns.

The problems concentrate among the larger campuses closest to homes.

It's very easy to predict based on two variables (size in MW and distance from residential clusters) whether a data center will create complaints.

Equipment matters too. A campus running gas turbines routinely is a different proposition from one with generators sitting idle for emergencies.

Cooling fans can also be a serious nuisance, but in general, turbines are worse. This is going to be a bigger problem going forward because more data centers are going "behind the meter" and building their own generation.

At Microsoft’s Mount Pleasant campus, the company found that cooling fans were creating a tonal noise and changed their operation. This substantially resolved the problem. 

Setbacks, equipment selection, silencers, barriers, and operating changes matter. “There’s a data center nearby” does not have to mean “you can’t sleep.”

How noisy are America’s largest data centers?

I had my agents crank on this question for over a week. Together we investigated the 25 largest operating US AI campuses (according to Epoch), looking at satellite imagery, equipment, nearby homes, and noise complaints.

I expected to dismiss resident concerns. I came away more sympathetic to the neighbors, but also convinced that these problems are avoidable.

My approach was to evaluate each data center with satellite imagery, look at filings and identify the loudest equipment (typically cooling towers or gas turbines), find the nearest cluster of 5+ homes, and measure that distance. 

From those distances and assumptions about the equipment and the terrain, I was able to derive a modeled noise estimate in dBA. I compared this against a history of verified complaints for each data center.

The main thing that shocked me was how close some of these absolutely enormous facilities are to neighborhoods.

11 of the 25 are less than 500 meters from a residential cluster. The closest is about 90 meters.

Contrary to what I thought, these are not all remote campuses in the middle of nowhere. Some are practically in people’s backyards.

Proximity isn’t destiny.

For 17 of the 25, I found no credible current operating noise complaint. 

Four had limited allegations or substantially remediated issues. Four had more substantial documented concerns.

The problems concentrate among the larger campuses closest to homes.

It's very easy to predict based on two variables (size in MW and distance from residential clusters) whether a data center will create complaints.

SpaceXAI's Colossus 2 in Mississippi was the worst case in the sample. It's also the biggest data center in America. 

An enormous campus, a large fleet of onsite gas turbines, and a residential cluster roughly 400 meters from the turbine source. Another group of homes is closer still to cooling equipment.

Resident complaints are extensively corroborated. This isn't generic anti-AI sentiment.

Compare that with AWS New Carlisle. 

It has 910 MW of  powered IT capacity, with the nearest qualifying residential cluster about 540 meters from the selected noise source.

I didn’t identify an ongoing operating-noise dispute there. It has other controversies, but noise doesn’t seem to be one of them.

Big and close does not automatically mean bad neighbor.

Equipment matters too. A campus running gas turbines routinely is a different proposition from one with generators sitting idle for emergencies.

Cooling fans can also be a serious nuisance, but in general, turbines are worse. This is going to be a bigger problem going forward because more data centers are going "behind the meter" and building their own generation.  

I modeled approximate sound levels at the homes using equipment assumptions, distance, and shielding. These are estimates, not measurements. Someone (who is not me) should do an acoustic study. No one has done one.

The simplest finding is the most intuitive: distance helps enormously.

Every site with a concern score of 3 or above (higher = noisier) was within 500 meters of a residential cluster. Every site at 800 meters or more scored 1.

That’s not a universal “800 meters is safe” rule. But residential separation is an easy place to start.

The encouraging part is that mitigation can work.

At Microsoft’s Mount Pleasant campus, the company found that cooling fans were creating a tonal noise and changed their operation. This substantially resolved the problem. 

Setbacks, equipment selection, silencers, barriers, and operating changes matter. “There’s a data center nearby” does not have to mean “you can’t sleep.”

My takeaway isn’t “data centers are harmless,” and it certainly isn’t “stop building them.” Noise is a real problem at some of the largest data centers in the US. 

Supporting the AI buildout doesn’t require dismissing its nearest neighbors. It will be much easier to defend if they can sleep through it.

Full analysis, methodology, and imagery:

Everything has happened before. Everything is repeated.

But the mistake that had the biggest effect on me was in 1982. I had calculated that American banks had lent a lot of money to a bunch of countries that would not be able to pay it back. Mexico defaulted in August 1982, and while I was right about that part, I was completely wrong about the market. I thought the stock market was going to go down, but it went up because the Federal Reserve eased.

I didn't just miss. I was publicly wrong and lost everything. I lost my company and all the people who worked for me—people who were like family. I was the only one left. I had to borrow $4,000 from my dad just to help pay my family bills.

It was one of the most painful experiences I have ever had, but it was also one of the best. It completely changed my attitude about decision-making. It taught me to move from thinking "I'm right" to asking myself, "How do I know I'm right?"
